Africa loses between $80bn and $125bn annually to illicit financial flows, with the losses accounting for about 25 per cent of the continent’s Gross Domestic Product, the African Union Advisory Board Against Corruption has said. The Chairperson of the board, Kwami Edem Senanu, disclosed this at the first General Assembly of the African Asset Recovery Practitioners’ Forum in Abuja on Tuesday. Senanu said the continent was losing approximately 50 per cent of its domestic revenue mobilisation to illicit financial flows, warning that the development was undermining efforts to address its socioeconomic challenges. He said while some United Nations partners estimated the annual losses at about $80bn, other stakeholders put the figure at approximately $125bn. “It is a fact that Africa continues to lose vast amounts of resources every year to corruption and illicit financial flows. Our UN partners quoted about $80bn annually. “Some other stakeholders on the continent look at about $125bn being lost annually just to illicit financial flows. Approximately, perhaps about 50 per cent of our domestic revenue mobilisation and 25 per cent of GDP is being lost,” he said. The AUABC chairperson said recovering stolen assets would provide African countries with resources to address critical infrastructure and social development deficits. “Asset recovery provides for us the door to address substantive socioeconomic deficits on our African landscape. It also provides for us an opportunity to build and provide hospitals, schools, and roads and to address other key challenges of our people,” he stated. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. He explained that the African Asset Recovery Practitioners’ Forum was established to provide a platform for experts, prosecutors and anti-corruption institutions across the continent to work together to tackle illicit financial flows and recover stolen assets. Speaking at the event, the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of the Federation, Lateef Fagbemi (SAN), called for a harmonised continental standard operating procedure for tracing, freezing, seizing, confiscating, repatriating and managing stolen assets across Africa. He said the framework should respect the domestic laws and sovereignty of member states while setting common minimum standards, clear channels for timely mutual legal assistance, secure information-sharing protocols and safeguards for due process and third-party rights. “Our objective must be simple, to make cooperation faster, recovery more effective, and the management of recovered wealth more transparent and accountable to the people of Africa,” he said. The minister also urged stronger beneficial ownership transparency, improved digital asset-tracing capabilities, professional training and independent reporting on how recovered assets were used. He stressed that asset recovery should not be judged only by the value of assets retrieved. “The success of our asset recovery efforts must not be measured solely by the monetary value of assets recovered, but by the transparency of the process, effective asset management, accountability, and the ultimate developmental benefit to our citizens,” Fagbemi said. Fagbemi said no country could tackle the concealment of criminal proceeds across borders alone. “No country can effectively address these challenges in isolation,” he said, calling for stronger cooperation and information exchange among national and international institutions. He welcomed the Forum’s decision to widen its reach beyond traditional law enforcement and anti-corruption bodies to include ministries of finance, tax authorities and revenue agencies. In his welcome address, the Chairman of the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission and Chair of the Interim Steering Council of the AARP-F, Dr Musa Aliyu (SAN), said the assembly offered an opportunity to reflect on progress since the Forum’s establishment, exchange professional experiences and agree on a common direction for its future. He said delegates would focus on three institutional milestones over the four days: validating the Forum’s Work Plan and Strategic Priorities, electing a Steering Council, and formally handing over from the Interim Steering Council to the new one.
